newsitem.title: USA: Republicans keep their grip on U.S. Congress.
newsitem.headline: Republicans keep their grip on U.S. Congress.

text.p: Republicans retained control of the Senate and House of Representatives in the U.S. congressional elections, putting President Bill Clinton on the defensive at the start of his second term.
It was the first time Republicans had won both houses of Congress for two consecutive elections since the 1920s. Republicans won both legislative chambers in 1994 for the first time in 40 years.

The Republicans Tuesday won open Senate seats previously held by Democrats in Alabama, Nebraska and Clinton's home state of Arkansas, where the party grabbed a Senate seat for the first time since the post-Civil War era.
Republicans lost one of their own -- three-term Sen. Larry Pressler of South Dakota, chairman of the commerce committee -- who was defeated by Democratic Representative Tim Johnson.

The current Senate lineup in the 100-seat Senate is 53 Republicans to 47 Democrats. Only the Oregon Senate race for the seat held by retiring Republican Mark Hatfield remained undecided among the 34 Senate races.

In the House, with more than a score of races undecided, the prospects were for a smaller majority for Republicans who held a 235-197 edge in the last Congress with one independent and two vacancies. House Speaker Newt Gingrich admitted early on Wednesday that Republicans had lost five to 10 seats, but that was short of the 19 seats required for a Democratic majority.
Most of the freshmen who swept to victory in the Republican takeover led by Gingrich two years ago were fending off challenges despite a powerful advertising campaign against them by labour unions.
The new congressional lineup was expected to be a force for compromise with neither Clinton nor the Republicans able to push through controversial legislation.
Both sides overreached in the last Congress -- Clinton with his failed healthcare reform plan and the Republicans with a budget plan that led to shutdown of the government.

In a victory statement in Marietta, Georgia, Gingrich said the elections had shown that "there's a real desire by the country for commonsense change towards a smaller government and decentralizing power out of Washington and lower taxes."
In the Arkansas Senate race, Republican Tim Hutchinson defeated Democrat Winston Bryant for the open seat held by retiring Sen. David Pryor to become the the state's first Republican senator.

In Alabama Republican Jeff Sessions defeated Democrat Roger Bedford for the seat held by retiring Democrat Howell Heflin, and in Nebraska Republican Chuck Hagel beat Democratic Gov. Ben Nelson for the seat of retiring Democrat James Exon.

Democrats won hard-fought races to retain seats in Massachusetts, New Jersey, Georgia and Illinois. Republicans kept two open seats in Kansas, vacated by presidential candidate Bob Dole and Sen. Nancy Kassebaum. They also won tough races to hold Senate seats in North and South Carolina, Tennessee, Maine, Colorado, Wyoming and Idaho.

Voters re-elected two of the Senate's most prominent conservatives -- Jesse Helms of North Carolina and 93-year-old Strom Thurmond of South Carolina who aims to celebrate his 100th birthday as a senator in six years.

Thurmond, who will be 94 on Dec. 5, fended off a challenge by Democrat Elliott Close, to head into his eighth six-year term. Helms defeated the black former mayor of Charlotte, Harvey Gantt, in a replay of their contest six years ago.
Their race was the most expensive among the Senate contests, according to the watchdog group Common Cause. Helms spent more than $19 million and Gantt more than $6 million.
In New Hampshire conservative Republican Bob Smith held off a strong challenge by Democrat Dick Swett.

In New Jersey Democratic Representative Robert Torricelli defeated conservative Republican Dick Zimmer for the Senate seat vacated by Democrat Bill Bradley. The race had been marked by furious mudslinging ads from both sides.

In Massachusetts Democratic Sen. John Kerry won a third term in a high-profile race with popular Gov. William Weld. In Illinois Representative Richard Durbin defeated Republican Al Salvi, winning the open seat vacated by Democrat Paul Simon.
In Georgia triple amputee Max Cleland, former head of the Veterans Administration, held the Senate seat vacated by fellow Democrat Sam Nunn, defeating Republican Guy Millner.
